title: How do we know two long-side lines are parallel?
description: The long side of a set square makes the same angle with l each time it slides, and a line is drawn along it twice. The two angles are named and compared, then checked by tracing one over the other or by measuring. Keeko doubts that a check by eye is enough.
teaching_notes: One idea: a sliding set square keeps its angle with l, so the corresponding angles are equal and the lines are parallel; tracing or a protractor checks it. Watch for students who trust the eye instead of tracing or measuring.

source: Place the long side of a 45° set square so that it makes 45°
video_script.why: The child uses the same test as the sliding set square, now with a slanting side, and learns two ways to check equal angles.
video_script.substitution: the book's own long side of a set square, placed at forty five degrees to l, drawn along twice
video_script.anchor: a line l, and the long side of a forty five degree set square drawn along twice as it slides
video_script.wrong_move: trusts the eye to see that the lines are parallel and does not trace or measure the angles
video_script.payoff_line: Equal corresponding angles make the lines parallel

final_answer.value: Yes, parallel: the corresponding angles are both 45°
final_answer.spoken: yes, the two lines are parallel, because the corresponding angles are both forty five degrees

maths_rules: the long side makes 45 degrees with l each time, because the set square slides and does not turn
l is the transversal, and the two angles of 45 degrees are corresponding angles
45 = 45, so the corresponding angles are equal
equal corresponding angles mean the two lines are parallel
check: trace one angle and slide it over the other, or measure both with a protractor
video_script.design: One line l and the slanting long side drawn in two positions, with the two forty five degree angles in the same corner. A tracing of one angle slides over the other in the check step.
